resources.string: MD5 or SHA-1 used where collision resistance is required; plain hash instead of a KDF for passwords; truncated digests.
SHA-256 used. No practical collision attack exists. NIST-approved for all integrity use cases.
MD5 used to verify file integrity. Collision attacks known since 2004 — attacker can produce two files with the same hash.
Full 256-bit (32-byte) SHA-256 output retained. 2^128 work required to find a collision.
SHA-256 output truncated to first 4 bytes (32 bits). Birthday attack finds collision with only ~65,000 hashes.
Password hashed with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (310,000 iterations + random salt). GPU cracking reduced by 6 orders of magnitude.
Password stored as SHA-256(password). Fast hash — 10 billion guesses/sec on a GPU. Offline cracking trivial.
